note: One entry per clip. 'segments' is the narration: one line per on-screen caption, in the order the captions appear in the scene.

segments.caption: A transformer cannot read text: it needs numbers.
segments.text: Take a short sentence from a clinical note: the patient has a cold. A transformer cannot work with text directly. Everything has to become numbers first.

segments.caption: A tokenizer splits the sentence into tokens.
segments.text: First, a tokenizer splits the sentence into tokens. Here we get five: the, patient, has, a, and cold.

segments.caption: Each token gets an integer ID from the tokenizer's vocabulary.
segments.text: Each token is mapped to an integer ID from the tokenizer's vocabulary. The exact numbers on screen are only illustrative.

segments.caption: Each ID looks up one row of a learned embedding table.
segments.text: Each ID selects one row of a learned embedding table, which has one row for every entry in the vocabulary. That row becomes the token's vector.

segments.caption: The five vectors stack into a 5 × d matrix: one row per token.
segments.text: Stacking the five vectors gives a five by d matrix, with one row per token. We draw d as four. In BERT base, d is seven hundred sixty-eight.

segments.caption: Problem: the token “cold” always gets the same vector.
segments.text: But there is a problem. The token cold always has the same ID, thirty-one forty-seven, so it always gets exactly the same vector.

segments.caption: But the meanings differ: an infection versus a temperature.
segments.text: In the patient has a cold, the word means an infection. In the patient feels cold, it means a low temperature. The embedding cannot tell them apart.

segments.caption: Attention fixes this by giving each token a vector that depends on its context.
segments.text: Attention solves this. It updates each token's vector using the other tokens in the sentence, so the vector depends on context.

segments.caption: Take the token “cold”: its query is compared with the key of every token.
segments.text: Let's follow the token cold. Its query vector, in red, is compared with the key vector of every token in the sentence, in green.

segments.caption: Each score is a dot product: how well that key matches the query.
segments.text: Each score is the query for cold dotted with a key, then divided by the square root of d. The scaled scores are minus zero point five, zero point two, one point three, zero point six, and one point six.

segments.caption: The highest scores go to “has” and to “cold” itself.
segments.text: The highest scores go to cold itself, at one point six, and to has, at one point three. These are the tokens that matter most here.

segments.caption: Softmax turns the scores into weights between 0 and 1 that sum to 1.
segments.text: A softmax turns the five scores into attention weights. They are all between zero and one, and together they sum to one.

segments.caption: The new vector for “cold” is the weighted sum of the five value vectors.
segments.text: The new vector for cold is the weighted sum of the five value vectors, in blue. The values of has and cold contribute the most.

segments.caption: Now 'cold' carries its context: has a cold means an infection.
segments.text: Now the vector for cold carries its context. In the phrase has a cold, the model can represent cold as an infection, not a temperature.

segments.caption: Attention ignores word order.
segments.text: Attention compares every token with every other token, but nothing in it knows which token came first. Chest pain, no pressure, and no pain, chest pressure contain the same five tokens, so attention alone cannot tell these two patients apart.

segments.caption: Fix: add a position vector to each token embedding.
segments.text: The fix is to give each position its own vector and add it to the token embedding before the first block. The same word at a different position now looks slightly different to the model.

segments.caption: Option 1: learn one vector per position (BERT).
segments.text: The simplest option is to learn one position vector per slot, just like the embedding table for words. BERT learns five hundred twelve of them, so it cannot read past five hundred twelve tokens.

segments.caption: Option 2: compute positions from waves (original transformer).
segments.text: The original transformer computes position vectors instead of learning them. It uses waves: a sine and a co-sine wave at a fast speed, and another sine and co-sine pair at a slow speed.

segments.caption: Read every wave at one position: those values are the position vector.
segments.text: To build the vector for position one, read the height of each wave at position one. The four heights, zero point eight four, zero point five four, zero point two five, and zero point nine seven, are the position vector.

segments.caption: Fast waves separate neighbors; slow waves separate distant positions.
segments.text: Move to position two and the fast waves change a lot, while the slow waves barely move, like the second hand and the hour hand of a clock. Together, they give every position its own pattern.

segments.caption: Both are added once, at the input.
segments.text: Learned or computed, these absolute positions are added once, at the input, and every later layer has to carry that information forward. Newer models handle position differently, inside attention itself.

segments.caption: What matters is often distance, not absolute position.
segments.text: For the meaning of chest pain, it matters that pain comes right after chest, not that chest is word two or word seven. Relative position methods build distance directly into attention.

segments.caption: RoPE rotates each query and key by an angle set by its position.
segments.text: Rotary position embeddings, or rope, do not add anything to the embedding. Instead, each query and key vector is rotated by an angle proportional to its position. Here, fifteen degrees per position.

segments.caption: The score depends only on the distance between the two tokens.
segments.text: After rotation, the score is zero point nine three. Now move the same phrase to positions seven and eight. Both arrows rotate further, but the angle between them is unchanged, so the score is still zero point nine three.

segments.caption: Farther apart means a different angle and a different score.
segments.text: If the two tokens are four positions apart, the angle between them grows, and the score drops to zero point two eight. Real models rotate many pairs of dimensions at different speeds, the same waves as before.

segments.caption: ALiBi: subtract a penalty that grows with distance.
segments.text: A simpler idea is Alibi. It leaves the vectors alone and subtracts a penalty from each attention score, proportional to distance. For cold, with a slope of zero point two five, the farthest token loses one, and cold itself loses nothing.

segments.caption: Nearby tokens gain weight; distant tokens lose it.
segments.text: After softmax, the weights shift toward nearby tokens: from zero point zero five, zero point one, zero point three, zero point one five, and zero point four, to zero point zero two, zero point zero six, zero point two four, zero point one five, and zero point five three.

segments.caption: Today: RoPE in nearly every open LLM.
segments.text: Today, rope is used in nearly every open large language model, including Llama, Kwen, DeepSeek, and Gemma, and even in newer encoders like Modern BERT. To read longer records than they were trained on, models stretch the rotation angles after pretraining.

segments.caption: The encoder starts from the token vectors plus position information.
segments.text: An encoder block starts from the five token vectors. Each one is combined with a position vector, because attention by itself ignores word order.

segments.caption: Multi-head self-attention lets every token look at every other token.
segments.text: Multi-head self-attention lets every token look at every other token. BERT base runs twelve attention heads in parallel, each with its own queries, keys, and values.

segments.caption: Add & normalize: the input is added back around attention, then normalized.
segments.text: Then comes add and normalize. A residual connection adds the block's input back to the attention output, and layer normalization keeps the values well scaled.

segments.caption: A feed-forward network then transforms each token on its own: d to 4d to d.
segments.text: Next, a feed-forward network transforms each token separately. It expands each vector from d to four d dimensions, then projects it back down to d.

segments.caption: A second add & normalize wraps the feed-forward network.
segments.text: A second add and normalize wraps the feed-forward network, again with a residual connection around it.

segments.caption: The output has the same shape as the input: one vector per token.
segments.text: The output has exactly the same shape as the input: five by d in, five by d out, with one updated vector per token.

segments.caption: Because shapes match, blocks stack: BERT-base uses 12 of them.
segments.text: Because the shapes match, blocks can be stacked one on top of another. BERT base stacks twelve encoder blocks, each with its own weights.
